name: HSBC case mid-window: the incoming transfer offsets the loan, the mortgage and the store loans (G481)

expected.notes: The same HSBC shape with the standing order and the mortgage both inside the period: today Wed 21 Oct 2026, payday Fri 30 Oct is 9 days away, so the window is days 0 to 8 (21 to 29 Oct). Barclays holds 2,300 and HSBC 150. Items: Barclays council tax 150 and HSBC personal loan 140 (both Thu 22 Oct, day 1); the standing order Barclays to HSBC 1,900 (Fri 23 Oct, day 2); HSBC mortgage 1,100 and store loans 450 (both Wed 28 Oct, day 7). The salary is due on payday, day 9, outside the window and not credited. Left to spend: pool 2,300 + 150 = 2,450; the standing order moves money inside the pool so both legs drop; day 1: - 150 - 140 = 2,160; day 7: - 1,100 - 450 = 610. Lowest point 610, so Left to spend 610. Barclays walk: 2,300 - 150 = 2,150 (day 1); day 2: - 1,900 = 250. After payments 250, low point 250, Spend from 250. Its balance after the order is 250, at or above zero, so the order is funded (G360 funded-inflow rule). HSBC walk: 150 - 140 = 10 (day 1); day 2: + 1,900 credited because Barclays is funded = 1,910; day 7: - 1,100 = 810; - 450 = 360. After payments 360. The lowest running balance is 10 (day 1, before the transfer lands), so low point 10, and Spend from is the smaller of the two, 10. After payments and low point differ here because the transfer lifts the balance after the low; the account is covered on both measures (no figure below zero), never covered and short together, and without the funded credit the mortgage would have read 10 - 1,100 - 450 = -1,540. No cover move; at risk 0. The period began Fri 25 Sep (day 27), so no payday plan. G436 (Kevin 2026-11-07, every account in isolation, money in vs money out), which supersedes the Left to spend and Spend from figures worked above where they differ: Each account on its own: Barclays 2,300 - 150 - 1,900 = 250; HSBC 150 - 140 + 1,900 - 1,100 - 450 = 360. 250 + 360 = 610, the same as the pooled figure: the 1,900 standing order is out on Barclays and in on HSBC, so it nets to zero. HSBC's own figure is its closing 360; the dip to 10 before the transfer lands is only a warning on the account (its low point), never part of the figure. G479 (Kevin 2026-11-19, option A: Left to spend is what can be spent without any payment failing; each account contributes its lowest balance before payday, money in counted only from its date), which supersedes the G436 figures above: Barclays 2,300 - 150 (day 1) - 1,900 (day 2) = 250, its lowest and closing figure. HSBC 150 - 140 (day 1) = 10, and only then does the 1,900 land (day 2, + 1,900 = 1,910), then - 1,100 = 810 and - 450 = 360. HSBC's lowest balance after a payment is 10, because the transfer arrives after the loan payment and cannot lift it, so HSBC contributes 10, not its 360 closing. 250 + 10 = 260 (was 610). This is a changed figure, not a bug: the transfer no longer nets to zero because HSBC has a payment before the credit lands (see the doctrine note in services/account_available.py). Neither account is below zero: no dip, no cover move. G481 (Kevin 2026-11-20), which supersedes the Left to spend and Spend from figures worked above where they differ: each account's Available = cash now - max(0, bills before payday - money in before payday); money in only offsets bills and never adds, and no timing is involved. Left to spend is the sum of the accounts, less plans on no account and the buffer (none here). Barclays: cash 2,300; bills 150 + 1,900 = 2,050; money in 0 (the salary is dated payday, Fri 30 Oct, outside the window): 250. HSBC: cash 150; bills 140 (loan) + 1,100 + 450 = 1,690; money in 1,900: 150 - max(0, 1,690 - 1,900) = 150, the transfer offsets the three payments and adds nothing, whenever it lands (it was 10, the low point after the mortgage, and before that 360). Left to spend 250 + 150 = 400. After payments stay 250 and 360 (150 + 1,900 - 1,690); low points 250 and 150; covered, no move, at risk 0.
